newsitem.title: USA: Pressure rises as US Airways, pilots set to meet.
newsitem.headline: Pressure rises as US Airways, pilots set to meet.

text.p: US Airways Group Inc will begin cutting unprofitable routes and may cancel a pending 400-aircraft order if it does not have a competitive cost structure in place by September 30, the pilots union said.
This looming deadline puts pressures on a new round of talks set to begin tomorrow in Washington. The pilots said there has been progress on some contract issues, but progress has been slow.

In a series of employee briefings earlier this month, US Airways turned up the heat on contract talks with the pilots. The Arlington, Va.-based airline told its employees it may cancel certain routes in Florida and at its Baltimore hub and ground some planes unless it can trim costs.
"They made it clear that they could start converting the company to a small, high-quality, continuously-shrinking regional airline," said Mark Thorpe, a media representative for the pilots union.

While US Airways has long said the the order for up to 400 Airbus Industrie jets in contingent on cutting costs, the company "had never said before that there was a September 30 deadline for the Airbus order," said Jon Bryan, chairman of the union's master executive council.
US Airways and Airbus officials could not be reached for comment.
"We clearly don't want to take any of management's concerns lightly .... but we do think there is some smoke and mirrors going on here," Bryan said.

The airline also is seeking wage cuts up to 12.5 percent from its pilots, which are among the highest paid in the industry. These demands come at a time pilots at rival carriers are seeing big pay increases.
US Airways pilots "would be delighted with cost of living increases, at this juncture," Bryan said.
Industry analysts said US Airways needs up to $1.5 billion in wage, salary and productivity concessions to bring its costs in line with other carriers.
Much of US Airways costs come from its inefficient route structure and its presence in the Northeast, has higher weather-related and operational costs, industry analysts said.
"Even if the pilots worked for nothing, seat mile costs would still be above our competitors," Bryan said.

US Airways also aims to form a low-cost unit to battle increasing competition from Southwest Airlines Co and Delta Air Lines Inc's Delta Express unit. But the airline and the pilots disagree on the scope of the new venture.
US Airways want the proposed low-cost unit to handle about 30 to 40 percent of its current flights.

The pilots said the company only faces competition from low-cost rivals on 5.5 percent of its business, so the new unit should be much smaller. The pilots want the low-cost unit to serve 10 percent of the company's routes, with additional growth possible if the airline can grow the mainline unit as well.
